title: Monetary Policy Surprises, Credit Costs, and Economic Activity
summary_en: How big are the financial-market consequences of monetary-policy shocks, and how do they translate into output and credit costs? Gertler and Karádi identify monetary surprises around FOMC announcements with high-frequency interest-rate movements and feed them into a structural VAR. They find that small policy shocks generate large movements in credit spreads and significant declines in real activity, suggesting that the credit channel — not just the standard interest-rate channel — is central to monetary-policy transmission.
data_used: US macroeconomic time series (industrial production, prices, credit spreads, term-structure variables) plus high-frequency surprises around FOMC dates extracted from federal-funds futures. Identification combines high-frequency external instruments with a structural VAR.
policy_relevance: Methodologically central to the MNB's monetary-policy research and to ECB watchers: the paper's high-frequency identification approach is the workhorse for measuring monetary-policy transmission in any small open economy, including Hungary. Practical implication for Hungarian forecasting: credit-spread responses to MNB rate decisions are quantitatively as important as the rate change itself for predicting GDP and inflation paths.
